profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an academic ML security lab preparing a 6-week experimental roadmap for a workshop paper on the security of transfer learning. The team wants to turn the seed topic into a concrete study centered on vulnerabilities introduced by common transfer-learning workflows rather than only model architectures. The agenda is to decide the experimental package for the first milestone: what counts as the baseline transfer-learning setup, which adaptation variants are included in the initial study, what results need to be ready for an internal review, who owns each workstream, and how the timeline maps onto the workshop submission schedule. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for a reproducible experimental sprint, an internal checkpoint date, and division of responsibilities between methodology design and implementation.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: ML security, adversarial robustness, empirical study design
members.background: Leads a university research group on secure and trustworthy machine learning, with prior work on data poisoning and benchmark methodology for vision models.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, publishable first milestone that can be shown to collaborators quickly, and is quietly worried that the project could sprawl into a broad survey of adaptation methods instead of a tight empirical paper.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'transfer learning baseline,' it naturally means the standard fine-tuning recipe used in papers: initialize from an ImageNet-pretrained checkpoint and fine-tune the final classifier with the backbone frozen except where explicitly noted.
An 'internal review next Friday' means a slide-ready package with stable numbers and polished plots circulated before the lab meeting, not merely partially completed experiment logs.

If they 'cover three downstream tasks,' that refers to three benchmark datasets representing different domains, each with the default single train/validation/test split and one canonical target label space.
Reproducing the baseline includes normal research-grade bookkeeping: fixed seeds, consolidated tables, and a short methods note, even if that is not separately assigned.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Transfer learning pipelines, large-scale experimentation, vision model implementation
members.background: Fourth-year PhD student who has built internal tooling for fine-tuning pretrained vision backbones and recently ran large adaptation sweeps for low-resource classification.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the project computationally feasible and align it with code he already has, while avoiding extra reporting overhead that would slow down experiment throughput.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'transfer learning baseline,' they usually mean the lab's existing adaptation pipeline: initialize from a public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tune the whole network with the standard low learning rate recipe unless otherwise specified.
An 'internal review next Friday' means having the main runs submitted or mostly completed so they can discuss trends live from the tracking dashboard; polished figures can wait until after feedback.
If they 'cover three downstream tasks,' that means three task families in the codebase, each potentially represented by multiple dataset variants or corruption subsets bundled under one task heading.
Reproducing the baseline mainly means code-level reproducibility and logged configs; writing methods notes and publication-style tables happens only once the experiment space is settled.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the transfer-learning baseline
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'start from the standard transfer-learning baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a conservative benchmark setup: pretrained backbone plus a newly trained head, with most of the backbone frozen so the paper can isolate methodology-specific security effects before expanding to deeper adaptation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the lab's standard implementation template: pretrained checkpoint with end-to-end fine-tuning of all layers at a low learning rate, because that is the default baseline in his pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are common enough in ML papers to sound interchangeable, and 'standard baseline' feels too routine to unpack in a planning meeting unless someone expects controversy.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of the three downstream tasks
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the first milestone should 'cover three downstream tasks.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means three concrete benchmark datasets, for example Flowers102, EuroSAT, and ChestX-ray14, each treated as one target problem.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means three categories of transfer setups already in the repository, such as natural-image classification, remote-sensing classification, and medical imaging, each of which may include multiple dataset variants or robustness subsets.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'task' is used loosely in ML labs to refer to either a dataset, a problem family, or a code module, so surface agreement sounds perfectly natural while hiding a materially different workload.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of ready for internal review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both commit to having results 'ready for internal review by next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready' means a curated packet: final plots, a one-page methods summary, and enough completed runs to support discussion of claims in a faculty-facing meeting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready' means the experiments are launched or substantially complete in the tracker, with preliminary dashboards sufficient for an informal technical check-in.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research settings, 'internal review' can refer either to a polished pre-read or a lab-progress discussion, and both participants assume the other shares their local norm from prior meetings.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Arjun will 'make the baseline reproducible' before expanding to attacks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes pinning seeds, packaging exact configs, summarizing dataset preprocessing choices, and producing a compact table that another lab member could rerun from notes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means ensuring the pipeline reruns from saved YAML configs and checkpoints inside the existing codebase, without extra documentation or publication-style artifact cleanup yet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as emphasizing rigor, but they operationalize reproducibility at different layers—research communication versus executable pipeline hygiene—so the phrase sounds aligned and responsible.

turns.inner_thought: I need this six-week plan to stay narrow enough to become a workshop paper quickly. If we let it drift into comparing every adaptation strategy under the sun, we'll lose the clean story. First milestone should be something collaborators can look at without caveats everywhere.

The main goal is to frame the security issues around transfer learning workflows, not just architecture choice, and get something we can show internally pretty quickly.

That gives us a clean transfer-learning baseline where any security effect is easier to attribute. I won't belabor it because 'standard transfer-learning baseline' should be obvious.
